strategies.title: Talk with young children — a lot, and back and forth
strategies.do: Make everyday conversation the first priority: name things, ask open questions, wait for answers, and build on what the child says. Nurseries and early-childhood settings should plan for rich adult–child talk every day.
strategies.why: Leading reviews put communication and language first in preparing children for reading. The Education Endowment Foundation's early-years evidence rates these approaches as having a very high impact for very low cost.

strategies.title: Read books together at home, and talk about them
strategies.do: Share a book most days: look at the pictures, talk about the story, let the child turn the pages and ask questions. Schools and libraries can show parents how, rather than only sending books home.
strategies.why: Shared book reading is the recommended centre of work with families of young children. Giving books away on its own is unlikely to help, but books combined with practical advice can.

strategies.title: Check children's eyesight before they learn to read
strategies.do: Make sure every young child has an eye check, and that children who are given glasses actually wear them in class and at home.
strategies.why: The early-years literacy guidance specifically calls for identifying possible eyesight problems and making sure treatment is used.

strategies.title: Teach sounds and letters clearly and in order
strategies.do: Teach children to hear the separate sounds in words, link those sounds to letters, and blend them to read and spell — step by step, every day, with plenty of practice.
strategies.why: International practice guides and the US National Reading Panel recommend explicit, systematic teaching of sound awareness and phonics in the first years of school. A major review of more than 300 studies explains why phonics is central in English, while stressing that children need more than phonics to become skilled readers.
strategies.caribbean: Barbados's national literacy programme uses this kind of structured approach; the Ministry reports reading gains in a sample of primary pupils, while cautioning that these are not national results.

strategies.title: Build vocabulary and the language of learning
strategies.do: Teach new words on purpose, use them in conversation, and give children chances to explain, retell and reason out loud — in class and at home.
strategies.why: Both major sets of guidance start with oral language: speaking, listening and vocabulary underpin reading comprehension later on.

strategies.title: Use the child's home language as a bridge to English
strategies.do: Where children arrive speaking Jamaican Creole or another Creole, value that language in class and use it to explain and discuss, while teaching Standard English literacy explicitly.
strategies.why: Jamaica's Language Education Policy recognises a bilingual situation. The University of the West Indies' Bilingual Education Project tested teaching literacy and content in both Jamaican and English in Grades 1–4 between 2004 and 2008.
strategies.caribbean: This is one of the region's most important open research questions, and a core focus of the Observatory's language and identity stream.

strategies.title: Give structured, early help to children who fall behind
strategies.do: Check reading progress regularly and give children who are struggling a well-designed, structured programme in small groups or one-to-one, delivered by trained staff.
strategies.why: High-quality structured interventions are a core recommendation for pupils who struggle with literacy.

strategies.title: Practise reading aloud until it flows
strategies.do: Give children daily, short practice reading real texts aloud, with feedback from a teacher, parent or older child, re-reading until the reading is accurate, smooth and expressive.
strategies.why: Fluency is one of the five components identified by the National Reading Panel. When word reading becomes automatic, attention is freed for understanding.

strategies.title: Teach vocabulary explicitly in every subject
strategies.do: Every teacher — science, history, maths — teaches the key words of their subject directly, and gives students repeated chances to use them.
strategies.why: Explicit vocabulary instruction is the first recommendation of the adolescent literacy practice guide.

strategies.title: Show students how good readers make sense of text
strategies.do: Model and practise strategies such as summarising, questioning and predicting, then gradually hand responsibility to students.
strategies.why: Direct, explicit teaching of comprehension strategies is recommended for students in upper primary and secondary school.

strategies.title: Make time for deep discussion of what students read
strategies.do: Plan regular, extended conversations about the meaning of texts, where students explain, challenge and justify their ideas.
strategies.why: Extended discussion of text meaning and interpretation is one of the practice guide's core recommendations.

strategies.title: Win back reluctant readers, especially boys
strategies.do: Offer choice of reading material, connect reading to students' interests and goals, and celebrate progress. Pay particular attention to boys' engagement.
strategies.why: Increasing motivation and engagement is a recommendation of the adolescent literacy guide.
strategies.caribbean: In PISA 2022, Jamaican girls outscored boys in reading by 35 points, so engagement strategies for boys matter here.

strategies.title: Offer intensive, individual support to teens who still struggle
strategies.do: Students who reach secondary school without secure reading need individual assessment and targeted teaching from a trained reading specialist.
strategies.why: Intensive, individualised intervention by trained specialists is recommended for struggling adolescent readers.

strategies.title: Support routines at home rather than doing homework for children
strategies.do: Help children keep a regular time and place for reading and homework, and show interest in what they learn. Encourage reading over the long school holidays.
strategies.why: Guidance on working with parents recommends supporting routines and good habits, and is cautious about direct help with homework for older children. Summer reading initiatives show promise.

strategies.title: Find out whether a struggling reader needs help with words, meaning, or both
strategies.do: Before choosing support, check two things separately: how well the learner reads words, and how well they understand language when it is read to them. Then target help at the weaker side.
strategies.why: The Simple View of Reading shows that reading comprehension depends on both word recognition and language comprehension, and that help works best when it targets the specific weakness.

strategies.title: Teach adults the building blocks of reading, explicitly
strategies.do: Adult programmes should assess each learner and teach the parts of reading they need — decoding, vocabulary, fluency and comprehension — with material that matters in their lives and work.
strategies.why: Systematic reviews of adult literacy instruction identify stronger and weaker findings and draw on school-age research where adult studies are thin. The evidence base for adults is smaller than for children.

strategies.title: Build adult and family literacy programmes that respect home languages
strategies.do: Design community and family literacy programmes around learners' languages and cultures, and learn from documented programmes elsewhere.
strategies.why: UNESCO's Institute for Lifelong Learning collects effective adult literacy practice, including approaches for multilingual and multicultural communities.
strategies.caribbean: Relevant across the region's Creole-speaking communities, including Haiti and the Kwéyòl-speaking Eastern Caribbean.

strategies.title: Design adult programmes so learners can keep coming back
strategies.do: Offer classes at times and places that fit work and family life — evenings, weekends, workplaces, churches and community centres — and keep in touch with learners who drop out so they can return.
strategies.why: Adults lead busy lives, and most stay in literacy programmes far less time than they need to make strong gains. Convenient times and places may be critical to helping them persist.

strategies.title: Teach reading and writing alongside job skills
strategies.do: Pair a literacy teacher with a trade or job-skills instructor so adults build reading, writing and maths while training for real work, instead of having to finish basic classes first.
strategies.why: In Washington State's I-BEST model, basic-skills and occupational instructors team-teach. Students were more likely than other basic-skills students to earn college credits and certificates and to improve their basic-skills test scores.
strategies.caribbean: This fits the Caribbean's strong vocational training systems, such as Jamaica's HEART/NSTA Trust.

strategies.title: Offer clear steps from basic literacy to a recognised qualification
strategies.do: Start each adult with a diagnostic assessment, place them at the right level, and give them a visible ladder of levels that leads to a certificate employers recognise.
strategies.why: Adults are more willing to invest time when the goal is concrete and the next step is clear.
strategies.caribbean: Jamaica's High School Diploma Equivalency programme has three levels, from Grade 1 up to Grades 10–11, leading to CXC-level work, and begins with a diagnostic test.

strategies.title: Use phones and computers to add practice, not to replace teaching
strategies.do: Give adults well-chosen apps, audio and online exercises to practise between classes, tied closely to what they learn with their teacher.
strategies.why: Research reviews find that technology does not produce learning on its own; it amplifies the teaching strategy behind it. Used well, it can free busy adults from having to be in one place to practise.

strategies.title: Help parents and children learn to read together
strategies.do: Run family literacy sessions where parents build their own reading and writing while learning simple ways to support their children's learning at home.
strategies.why: UNESCO guidance on family literacy holds that it is never too early or too late to learn to read, and that parents with weak literacy skills need targeted support to help their children.

strategies.title: Take literacy classes into the workplace
strategies.do: Partner with employers to offer literacy and numeracy classes on site or at shift change, using real workplace materials.
strategies.why: Workplace delivery removes travel and timing barriers, which matter greatly for adult persistence.
strategies.caribbean: Jamaica's adult education agency deployed its high-school equivalency programme through a dedicated workplace unit.

science.intro: Decades of international research — often called the science of reading — explain how people learn to read and why some struggle. Three ideas sit at its core.

models.title: The Simple View of Reading
models.text: Understanding what you read depends on two things multiplied together: reading the words on the page, and understanding the language they express. If either is weak, understanding suffers, and neither is enough on its own.

models.title: The Reading Rope
models.text: Each side is made of strands. Word recognition grows from awareness of sounds, decoding, and recognising familiar words by sight. Language comprehension grows from background knowledge, vocabulary, sentence and text structure, reasoning, and knowledge of how texts work. With practice the strands become tightly woven into skilled reading.

models.title: Five components of reading instruction
models.text: A major US review of reading research identified five areas that effective early reading teaching covers: awareness of the sounds in words, phonics, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension.

science.caribbean: Most of this research comes from English-speaking countries where children's home language is English. In the Caribbean many children grow up speaking a Creole, so the language-comprehension side of reading needs particular care. How best to bridge home language and the language of school is one of the Observatory's priority research questions.
science.beyond: A review of more than 300 studies concludes that phonics is central for learning to read English, but that becoming an expert reader takes much more: wide reading, rich vocabulary and knowledge, built over many years.
